pharm: Dibenzoxazepine antipsychotic; exact mechanism unestablished but associated with reduced excitability of subcortical inhibitory areas and dopamine receptor antagonism.
quick: Start 10 mg twice daily; usual range 60-100 mg/day; max 250 mg/day
May be taken without regard to meals
Third-trimester use risks neonatal EPS/withdrawal; use only if benefit justifies risk
Avoid if clinically possible; human milk levels unknown
Use with caution; renal failure reported after overdose
EPS, tardive dyskinesia, CBC, prolactin symptoms, fall risk, mental status
summary: Loxapine is a conventional (typical) antipsychotic of the dibenzoxazepine class indicated for the treatment of schizophrenia. It is usually given in divided doses two to four times daily and titrated to a usual therapeutic range of 60 to 100 mg/day, not exceeding 250 mg/day. It carries a boxed warning: elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis treated with antipsychotic drugs are at increased risk of death, and loxapine is not approved for dementia-related psychosis. Key risks include extrapyramidal symptoms, tardive dyskinesia, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, seizures (lowers seizure threshold), leukopenia/agranulocytosis, anticholinergic effects, orthostatic hypotension, and falls.

dosage.d: 10 mg twice daily (up to 50 mg/day total in severely disturbed patients)
dosage.n: Increase fairly rapidly over the first 7-10 days until symptoms are controlled
Doses higher than 250 mg/day are not recommended

dosage.d: Reduce to lowest effective dose; many maintained at 20-60 mg/day

admin: Administer in divided doses, usually two to four times daily
Adjust dosage to individual patient needs based on symptom severity and prior antipsychotic response
Titrate fairly rapidly over the first 7-10 days to control symptoms, then reduce to the lowest effective maintenance dose
Warn ambulatory patients about activities requiring alertness and concomitant alcohol/CNS depressants
moa: Loxapine is an antipsychotic whose exact mode of action has not been established. Changes in the excitability of subcortical inhibitory areas have been observed in animals in association with calming and suppression of aggressive behavior, consistent with dopamine receptor antagonism characteristic of conventional antipsychotics.

absolute: Comatose or severe drug-induced CNS-depressed states (alcohol, barbiturates, narcotics)
relative: Elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis (boxed warning: increased mortality; not approved)
History of seizures or convulsive disorders (loxapine lowers seizure threshold)
Glaucoma or urinary retention tendency (anticholinergic action)
Pre-existing low WBC or history of drug-induced leukopenia/neutropenia
monitor: CBC in patients with low WBC or prior drug-induced leukopenia/neutropenia
Orthostatic blood pressure and fall risk

preg: Neonates exposed to antipsychotic drugs during the third trimester are at risk for extrapyramidal and/or withdrawal symptoms (agitation, hypertonia, hypotonia, tremor, somnolence, respiratory distress, feeding disorder) following delivery, which may range from self-limited to requiring intensive care. Safe use in pregnancy has not been established; use only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus.
lact: The extent of excretion of loxapine or its metabolites in human milk is unknown, although loxapine and its metabolites are transported into the milk of lactating dogs. Administration to nursing women should be avoided if clinically possible.
renal: No specific renal dosing adjustment is provided. Use with caution; renal failure has been reported following loxapine overdose.
hepatic: No specific hepatic dosing adjustment is provided. Hepatocellular injury (SGOT/SGPT elevation) and rarely jaundice/hepatitis have been reported; use with caution.

major: Lorazepam: rare reports of significant respiratory depression, stupor, and/or hypotension with concomitant use
moderate: CNS-active drugs / CNS depressants: additive depression - use caution (not systematically evaluated)
Anticholinergic antiparkinson agents: additive anticholinergic effects (glaucoma, urinary retention)
Epinephrine: pressor effect may be reversed by loxapine; avoid for loxapine-induced hypotension
interactions.food: May be taken without regard to meals.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid; additive CNS depression and impaired alertness.
interactions.diagnostics: Elevates prolactin; may mask signs of overdose of other drugs and conditions such as intestinal obstruction or brain tumor due to its antiemetic effect.

common: Extrapyramidal symptoms (tremor, rigidity, akathisia, masked facies)

monitoring: Extrapyramidal symptoms and tardive dyskinesia (especially long-term/high-dose, elderly women)
CBC in patients with low WBC or history of drug-induced leukopenia/neutropenia; discontinue at first sign of WBC decline
Signs of NMS (hyperpyrexia, rigidity, autonomic instability)
Orthostatic blood pressure and fall risk
Mental and physical alertness, especially early in therapy
counsel: May cause drowsiness, especially when starting; avoid driving or operating machinery until you know how it affects you
Avoid alcohol and other sedating medications
Rise slowly to reduce dizziness from low blood pressure
Report abnormal involuntary movements (face, tongue, mouth), high fever with muscle stiffness, or signs of infection such as sore throat or fever
Long-term use carries a risk of tardive dyskinesia; attend follow-up appointments
pk: Sedation within 20-30 minutes; most pronounced at 1.5-3 hours
Rapidly cleared from plasma; extensively metabolized, mostly excreted within 24 hours
Effects lasted through ~12 hours in normal volunteers
Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F); dispense in a tight, child-resistant container
pearls: Conventional dibenzoxazepine antipsychotic; carries the antipsychotic-class boxed warning for increased mortality in elderly dementia patients
Lowers seizure threshold - use with extreme caution in patients with convulsive disorders
Avoid epinephrine for loxapine-induced hypotension; use norepinephrine or phenylephrine instead
Antiemetic effect may mask overdose of other drugs and conditions like intestinal obstruction
Available as loxapine succinate capsules dosed in loxapine base equivalents (5, 10, 25, 50 mg)
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as remembered. If it is almost time for the next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and continue the regular divided-dose schedule. Do not take two doses at once.
overdose: Signs range from mild CNS and cardiovascular depression to profound hypotension, respiratory depression, and unconsciousness; extrapyramidal symptoms, seizures, and renal failure may occur. Treatment is symptomatic and supportive: early gastric lavage and possibly extended dialysis. Avoid emesis (aspiration risk and antiemetic effect) and analeptics that may provoke convulsions. Treat severe hypotension with norepinephrine or phenylephrine - DO NOT use epinephrine (may further lower blood pressure). Treat severe EPS with anticholinergic antiparkinson agents or diphenhydramine; provide oxygen, IV fluids, and anticonvulsants as indicated.
